title: The Fish That Is a Battery

pages.text: Open the back of a torch and you will find the batteries lying end to end, the top of one touching the bottom of the next. Each one is an electric cell, and each gives a push of 1.5 volts. Lined up like this, three cells push together with 4.5 volts, enough to light the bulb brightly. Joining cells end to end is called connecting them in series. People worked out this trick about two hundred years ago. A fish in the rivers of South America has been using it for millions of years.

pages.text: Two words describe electricity in a wire. Voltage is the push that drives electric charge along, and it is measured in volts (V). Current is the flow of that charge, and it is measured in amperes (A). Nothing flows unless there is a complete loop from one end of the cell, through the wire and the bulb, and back to the other end. That loop is called a circuit. Break it anywhere, as a switch does, and the current stops at once. Adding more cells in series adds their voltages together, so the push is bigger and the current is larger.

That loop is called a circuit.

Adding more cells in series adds their voltages together, so the push is bigger and the current is larger.

pages.text: The electric eel can grow longer than a tall man. In spite of its name, it is not a true eel. It belongs to a group called knifefish. Most of its long body is filled with thousands of flat cells, stacked like coins in a roll. Each one produces only about 0.15 volts. But they are joined in series, and 5,000 of them firing together give about 750 volts. In 2019, scientists in Brazil measured one kind of electric eel giving 860 volts, the strongest shock recorded from any animal. The wall sockets in a Ghanaian home supply only 230 volts.

pages.text: The eel lives in muddy water and sees poorly, so it uses electricity in two ways. Weak pulses work like a torch in the dark: they help it to sense what is nearby and make hidden fish twitch. Then a burst of strong pulses stuns the prey so that the eel can swallow it. The water itself completes the circuit between the head and tail of the eel. Africa has a shocking fish too. The electric catfish lives in rivers across West Africa, including the Volta. Fishermen know it well and handle it with great care.

pages.text: Electric fish puzzled scientists in Europe. In Italy, Luigi Galvani found that the legs of a dead frog kicked when metal touched them. Another Italian, Alessandro Volta, studied the electric organs of fish and saw how they were stacked. In 1800 he announced his own stack: discs of two different metals, separated by cloth soaked in salt water. It gave a steady electric current, and it was the first battery. The volt is named in his honour. Ghana’s River Volta is not. Its name comes from a Portuguese word meaning a turn or bend.

pages.text: Why does a shock make muscles jump? Because your own body runs on electricity. Nerves carry tiny electrical signals from the brain to the muscles, and these signals tell the heart when to beat. A strong current from outside swamps those signals. Muscles lock, breathing can stop, and the heart can lose its rhythm. That is how the eel stuns a fish, and it is why mains electricity can kill. Never touch a switch or a socket with wet hands. Never push metal into a socket. And never go near a wire that has fallen to the ground.

activities.question: Three 1.5-volt cells are connected in series. What is the total voltage?
What must be true before a current can flow?
options: There must be a complete circuit
The wire must be very long

activities.question: How does an electric eel produce such a high voltage?
options: Thousands of small cells are joined in series, so their voltages add up
One very large cell produces all of it

activities.question: Apply it: A wire has fallen from a pole after a storm and lies across a path. What should you do?
options: Stay well away, warn other people, and tell an adult or the electricity company
Move it off the path with a dry stick

activities.prompt: Put these in order, from the lowest voltage to the highest.
items: One flat cell inside an electric eel (about 0.15 V)
Three torch batteries in series (4.5 V)
A wall socket in Ghana (230 V)
The strongest electric eel measured (860 V)

activities.definition: A complete loop that an electric current can flow around.
distractors: A round switch on a wall
The push that drives an electric current

glossary.definition: A device that pushes electric charge around a circuit; several joined together make a battery.
Joined end to end, so that the voltages add together.
The push that drives electric charge along, measured in volts.
The flow of electric charge, measured in amperes.
A complete loop that an electric current can flow around.
Two or more cells joined together.
